name: Friendly Spiders
description: Mars is home to an unusual species of spiders — Binary spiders. Right now, Martian scientists are observing a colony of $$$n$$$ spiders, the $$$i$$$-th of which has $$$a_i$$$ legs. Some of the spiders are friends with each other. Namely, the $$$i$$$-th and $$$j$$$-th spiders are friends if $$$\gcd(a_i, a_j) \ne 1$$$, i. e., there is some integer $$$k \ge 2$$$ such that $$$a_i$$$ and $$$a_j$$$ are simultaneously divided by $$$k$$$ without a remainder. Here $$$\gcd(x, y)$$$ denotes the greatest common divisor (GCD) of integers $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$. Scientists have discovered that spiders can send messages. If two spiders are friends, then they can transmit a message directly in one second. Otherwise, the spider must pass the message to his friend, who in turn must pass the message to his friend, and so on until the message reaches the recipient. Let's look at an example. Suppose a spider with eight legs wants to send a message to a spider with $$$15$$$ legs. He can't do it directly, because $$$\gcd(8, 15) = 1$$$. But he can send a message through the spider with six legs because $$$\gcd(8, 6) = 2$$$ and $$$\gcd(6, 15) = 3$$$. Thus, the message will arrive in two seconds. Right now, scientists are observing how the $$$s$$$-th spider wants to send a message to the $$$t$$$-th spider. The researchers have a hypothesis that spiders always transmit messages optimally. For this reason, scientists would need a program that could calculate the minimum time to send a message and also deduce one of the optimal routes.
input_specification: The first line of input contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 3\cdot10^5$$$) — the number of spiders in the colony. The second line of input contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 3\cdot10^5$$$) — the number of legs the spiders have. The third line of input contains two integers $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le s, t \le n$$$) —the spiders between which the message must be sent.
output_specification: If it is impossible to transmit a message between the given pair of spiders, print $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, in the first line of the output print the integer $$$t$$$ ($$$t \ge 1$$$) — the number of spiders that participate in the message transmission (i. e. the minimum time of message delivery in seconds plus one). In the second line, print $$$t$$$ different integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_t$$$ ($$$1 \le b_i \le n$$$) — the ids of the spiders through which the message should follow, in order from sender to receiver. If there are several optimal routes for the message, output any of them.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1775D — Friendly Spiders [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
